          1. Delay condoned.

          2. This Miscellaneous Application is filed by the Union of India,

                   seeking clarification of the common judgment dated 12.02.2026

                   passed in C.A. Nos.6820-6824 of 2018 (Union of India Through

                   Its Secretary & Ors. v. SGT Girish Kumar & Ors.) (‘the common

                   judgment’) by which this Court dismissed the appeals preferred

                   by Union of India and allowed the appeals preferred by the ex-

                   servicemen. By the common judgment, ex-servicemen were held

                   entitled to disability pension, including the benefit of broad

                   banding w.e.f. 01.01.1996 or 01.01.2006, as the case may be,

                   along with interest at the rate of 6 % per annum. The objections

                   of the applicant founded on limitation, delay and laches were not

          3. Mrs. Archana Pathak Dave, learned Additional Solicitor General,
                                                                                   1
  submitted that in the batch of appeals decided by this Court vide

  common judgment, the entitlement of Ex-Servicemen to the

  disability element of the pension was never in dispute. It was

  contended that the ex-servicemen in the aforesaid batch of

  appeals were already in receipt of disability pension and had

  merely sought its re-computation by way of broad banding. It was

  urged that the common judgment was rendered in the specific

  factual context of the appeals before this Court and was not

  intended to unsettle the principles governing stale or belated

  pensionary claims.

4. Learned Additional Solicitor General had furnished particulars

  of 23 cases pertaining to Air Force and 26 cases of Army which

  either have been decided or are pending before the High Court or

  the Armed Forces Tribunal (AFT) after the passing of the common

  judgment. It was pointed out that in several cases, the final

  orders passed earlier, which had restricted the benefit of arrears

  and were complied with by the applicant, have been modified by

  placing reliance on the common judgment. It was contended that

  the common judgment is being relied upon in cases involving

  pensionary claims of ex-servicemen which do not fall in the

  category of appeals decided by this Court. It was urged that a

  mechanical application of the common judgment would result in

                                                                   2
  administrative and financial implications and would unsettle the

  matters which have attained finality. It was, therefore, prayed

  that the common judgment be clarified and it be directed that the

  common judgment should not be mechanically extended to all

  pensionary claims where the entitlement of pension itself was in

  dispute and was later settled by Courts/Tribunals.

5. Mr. M.V.R. Mukunda, learned counsel for the respondents, on

  the other hand fairly submitted that in the common judgment,

  arrears from specified dates were granted to ex-servicemen who

  were already in receipt of disability pension and were seeking

  only its re-computation. It was contended that the question of

  delay cannot be examined in isolation from the conduct of Union

  of India. By way of an illustration, it was demonstrated that in a

  case decided by Allahabad High Court, the ex-serviceman retired

  on 31.10.2011 and preferred the appeal claiming disability

  pension on 30.11.2011. It was pointed out that the said appeal

  was decided on 11.02.2017 that is after six years, and thus, the

  original application filed before the Tribunal on 30.04.2018, was

  well within time. It was further pointed out that the applicant

  itself approached court belatedly and therefore cannot claim

  equity on the ground of delay and laches.

6. We have considered the rival submissions and have perused the

                                                                   3
   record.

7. It is well-settled in law that the observations made in a judgment

   are not to be read as provisions of a statute, nor are they to be

   read divorced from the context of the facts in which they were

   made. A difference in facts may make a material difference to the

   precedential value of a decision1.

8. In the light of aforesaid established legal principles, we only wish

   to state that the common judgment dated 12.02.2026 passed in

   Civil Appeal Nos. 6820-6824 of 2018 cannot be construed to

   mean that on the basis of said judgment grant of disability

   pension with arrears can be claimed in every case. Needless to

   state that each claim shall be decided on its own merits.

9. Accordingly, the Miscellaneous Application is disposed of.

            11.        Before we proceed to interpret the Agreement in

            question for the purposes of determining whether the

            Delhi High Court had the jurisdiction to appoint the

            arbitrator, it would be useful to consider a few decisions

            wherein a distinction between the “seat” of arbitration

            and the “venue” for arbitral proceedings has been carved

            out.

            12.        In Indus Mobile (supra), this Court held that

            seat is akin to an exclusive jurisdiction clause. It was

            held that under the Law of Arbitration, unlike the Code

            of Civil Procedure, which applies to suits filed in courts,

            a reference to “seat” is a concept by which a neutral

            venue can be chosen by the parties to an arbitration

            agreement. The neutral venue may not, in the classical

            sense, have jurisdiction, that is, no part of the cause of

            action may have arisen at the neutral venue, and neither

            would any of the provisions of Sections 16 to 21 of CPC

            be attracted. However, the moment the “seat” is

            determined, the courts wherein the seat is located would

            19.        However, when an agreement specifies the place

            of arbitration and simultaneously confers exclusive

            jurisdiction on courts located at a place other than the

            one specified for arbitration, a question would arise

            whether the place of arbitration is just a “venue” or the

            “juridical seat”.

            of this Court delineated the tests as to when “venue” can

            paragraphs of the judgment are extracted below:

                       “58. Thus, this court in BGS SJS SOMA laid down a
                       three-condition test as to when “venue” can be construed
                       as “seat” of arbitration. The conditions that are required
                       to be fulfilled are as under:

                                     question should designate or mention only

                              (ii)   Such place must have anchored the arbitral
                                     proceedings i.e. the arbitral proceedings

                       construed as the “seat” of arbitration. It is clarified that,

            21.        In the present case, a plain reading of the

            arbitration clause would indicate that Delhi is not the

            only place specified for arbitration. Both Delhi and Goa

            the place specified i.e. venue for arbitral proceeding

            38 of the Agreement would be helpful in determining the

            juridical seat. Since Clause 38 of the Agreement confers

            exclusive jurisdiction to the courts at Goa and Clause

            32.5 provides that arbitration proceedings will be held in

            Goa, it is clear that the parties have agreed that Goa

            22.        The submission on behalf of the appellant that

            the arbitration agreement is independent of the main

            aforesaid proposition. Here, the arbitration clause itself

            mentions two places. One of those two has been chosen

            by the parties for the courts located therein to have

            exclusive jurisdiction. In such a situation, to determine

            the juridical seat, the Governing law clause 38 cannot

            be ignored.         Similarly, in the Delhi High Court decision

8.    We have considered the rival submissions advanced by learned counsel

appearing for the parties and have perused the material placed on record.



9.    The controversy before us essentially concerns the permissibility of the

amendment sought by the original plaintiff under Order VI Rule 17 of the CPC.

For ease reference, the said provision is extracted below:

      “Amendment of Pleadings.

      The Court may at any stage of the proceedings allow either party to alter or
      amend his pleadings in such manner and on such terms as may be just, and all
      such amendments shall be made as may be necessary for the purpose of
      determining the real questions in controversy between the parties:

      Provided that no application for amendment shall be allowed after the trial has
      commenced, unless the Court comes to the conclusion that in spite of due
      diligence, the party could not have raised the matter before the commencement
      of trial.”




10.   A plain reading of the aforesaid provision makes it clear that Order VI

Rule 17 of the CPC confers a discretionary power upon the Court to permit

amendments which are necessary for determining the real questions in

controversy between the parties. However, once the trial has commenced, the

exercise of such power is subject to the additional requirement that the Court

must be satisfied that despite due diligence, the party could not have raised the

matter before the commencement of trial. The object of the provision is to

enable the Court to effectively and completely adjudicate upon the dispute

between the parties, while at the same time, ensuring that a party does not
                                                                                11


introduce at a belated stage, matters which could, with due diligence, have been

raised earlier.



11.      The principles governing the exercise of jurisdiction under Order VI Rule

17 of the CPC are well settled. In A.K. Gupta & Sons Ltd. v. Damodar Valley

Corporation (supra), this Court explained that an amendment which introduces

a new case or a new cause of action is generally impermissible, particularly

where the new claim is barred by limitation. At the same time, where the

amendment does not introduce a new cause of action or a different case, but

merely sets out a different or additional approach to the same facts, such

amendment may be permitted. The Court thus drew a distinction between an

amendment introducing a new cause of action and one which merely elaborates

or alters the approach to the case already pleaded.

11.1. In Rajesh Kumar Aggarwal & others v. K.K. Modi and others 7 , this

Court held that the “real controversy test” is the basic and cardinal test

governing an application under Order VI Rule 17. The Court is required to

determine whether the proposed amendment is necessary for deciding the real

question in controversy between the parties, while ensuring that such

amendment does not cause injustice or prejudice to the opposite party.

11.2. Similarly, in Abdul Rahman and another v. Mohd. Ruldu and others

(supra), this Court reiterated that amendments necessary for determining the real

alter the basic nature of the suit. A change in the relief sought does not, by itself,

amount to a change in the nature of the suit. The following paragraph from the

said judgment is pertinent:

         “18. We reiterate that all amendments which are necessary for the purpose of
         determining the real questions in controversy between the parties should be
         allowed if it does not change the basic nature of the suit. A change in the nature
         of relief claimed shall not be considered as a change in the nature of suit and
         the power of amendment should be exercised in the larger interests of doing full
         and complete justice between the parties.”



11.3. In Revajeetu Builders and Developers v. Narayanaswamy and Sons &

others8, this Court held that although the Courts have wide discretion in matters

of amendment of pleadings, such discretion must be exercised judiciously and

with great care. The Court further culled out certain factors to be taken into

consideration while allowing or rejecting an application for amendment, which

include the following:

          “63. On critically analysing both the English and Indian cases, some basic principles
         emerge which ought to be taken into consideration while allowing or rejecting the
         application for amendment:

         (1) whether the amendment sought is imperative for proper and effective adjudication
         of the case;

         (2) whether the application for amendment is bona fide or mala fide;

         (3) the amendment should not cause such prejudice to the other side which cannot be
         compensated adequately in terms of money;

         (4) refusing amendment would in fact lead to injustice or lead to multiple litigation;

11.4. In Life Insurance Corporation of India v. Sanjeev Builders Private

Limited and another 9 , this Court, while recognising the liberal approach to

amendments, also delineated circumstances in which an amendment may be

declined, including where a time-barred claim is sought to be introduced, the

nature of the suit is changed, or a valid defence of the opposite party is sought to

be taken away. The Court cautioned against adopting a hyper-technical

approach and emphasised that amendments which facilitate effective

adjudication of the dispute and avoid multiplicity of proceedings ought

ordinarily to be permitted, subject to the absence of injustice or prejudice to the

opposite party. The following conclusions are apposite:

         “71.2. All amendments are to be allowed which are necessary for determining

(c) The amendment does not raise a time-barred claim, resulting in divesting of

71.4. A prayer for amendment is generally required to be allowed unless:

71.4.1. By the amendment, a time-barred claim is sought to be introduced, in
which case the fact that the claim would be time-barred becomes a relevant
factor for consideration.

71.4.2. The amendment changes the nature of the suit.

71.4.4. By the amendment, the other side loses a valid defence.

71.5. In dealing with a prayer for amendment of pleadings, the court should
avoid a hypertechnical approach, and is ordinarily required to be liberal
especially where the opposite party can be compensated by costs.

71.6. Where the amendment would enable the court to pin-pointedly consider the
dispute and would aid in rendering a more satisfactory decision, the prayer for
amendment should be allowed.

71.7. Where the amendment merely sought to introduce an additional or a new
approach without introducing a time-barred cause of action, the amendment is
liable to be allowed even after expiry of limitation.

71.8. Amendment may be justifiably allowed where it is intended to rectify the
absence of material particulars in the plaint.

71.9. Delay in applying for amendment alone is not a ground to disallow the
prayer. Where the aspect of delay is arguable, the prayer for amendment could
be allowed and the issue of limitation framed separately for decision.

71.10. Where the amendment changes the nature of the suit or the cause of
action, so as to set up an entirely new case, foreign to the case set up in the
plaint, the amendment must be disallowed. Where, however, the amendment
sought is only with respect to the relief in the plaint, and is predicated on facts
which are already pleaded in the plaint, ordinarily the amendment is required to
be allowed.

71.11. Where the amendment is sought before commencement of trial, the court
is required to be liberal in its approach. The court is required to bear in mind
the fact that the opposite party would have a chance to meet the case set up in
amendment. As such, where the amendment does not result in irreparable
prejudice to the opposite party, or divest the opposite party of an advantage
which it had secured as a result of an admission by the party seeking
amendment, the amendment is required to be allowed. Equally, where the
amendment is necessary for the court to effectively adjudicate on the main issues
in controversy between the parties, the amendment should be allowed.”

11.5. More recently, in Akkiraju Panduranga Rao and another v. Gunlapally

Ranga Rao 10 , this Court reiterated that the principal considerations while

deciding an application for amendment are, first, whether the amendment is

necessary for determining the real question in controversy and secondly,

whether it can be allowed without causing injustice or prejudice to the opposite

amendment, courts should adopt a liberal approach and should not be unduly

concerned with technicalities.

11.6. In light of the statutory framework and the principles enunciated above,

we may now examine the permissibility of the amendment sought by the

original plaintiff.



12.      In the present case, there is no dispute that the application for amendment

was filed after commencement of the trial and therefore, the proviso to Order VI

Rule 17 of the CPC is attracted. The fact that the amendment was sought at a

belated stage is, by itself, not determinative. The principal question is whether,

the appellants have shown that despite due diligence, the matters now sought to

be introduced could not have been raised before the commencement of the trial.

The further question is whether the proposed amendment would fundamentally

alter the nature and character of the suit.

13.    As regards the requirement of due diligence, the original suit concerns the

right, title and interest in and possession of the very property which forms the

subject matter of the proposed amendment. The proposed pleading relating to

the compromise decree passed in T.S. No.105 of 1998 arises from the allegation

that the said decree affects a portion of the very suit property, namely, Ac. 0.02

decimals comprised in Hal Plot No.3371 / 4050. The case of the original

plaintiff is that he was not a party to the said suit and was unaware of the

compromise decree. It is stated that only upon obtaining certified copies of the

plaint and final decree on 22.06.2020, did he come to know of the compromise

in respect of suit plot No.3371 / 4050 measuring Ac. 0.04 decimals along with

other properties between Defendant No.8 and others. It is further stated that the

written statement filed by Defendant Nos.9 and 10 did not disclose the source of

title of their vendors.

13.1. The significance of these circumstances cannot be overlooked. The

proposed amendment is not founded upon a transaction or an event wholly

unconnected with the subject matter of the suit, but upon a subsequent discovery

of a decree which, according to the original plaintiff, has a bearing upon the title

to a portion of the very property in dispute. The record indicating that certified

copies of the plaint and final decree were obtained on 22.06.2020 is a relevant

circumstance in assessing the plea of due diligence. At this stage, it is not

necessary for the Court to finally determine whether the plaintiff’s assertion

regarding the date of knowledge is ultimately correct. What is required is to
                                                                                 17


examine whether sufficient explanation has been furnished for not raising the

matter before commencement of the trial.

13.2. Having regard to the aforesaid circumstances, we are of the view that the

explanation furnished by the appellants cannot, at this stage, be characterised as

a mere omission, inadvertence or negligence. The subsequent discovery of the

compromise proceedings, coupled with the assertion that the original plaintiff

was not a party to those proceedings and that the source of title of the vendors

was not disclosed in the written statement, provides a sufficient basis for

accepting the plea of due diligence for the purposes of the proviso to Order VI

Rule 17 of the CPC. The statutory requirement is therefore satisfied.



14.     The next question is whether the proposed amendment fundamentally

alters the nature and character of the suit. In our view, it does not. The original

suit is founded upon the plaintiff’s claim to title, possession and related reliefs

in respect of the suit property. The proposed amendment seeks to place before

the Court facts concerning a compromise decree which, according to the original

plaintiff, affects a portion of that very property and consequently bears upon the

rights claimed in the suit. The proposed amendment may enlarge the factual and

legal questions requiring adjudication; however, such enlargement cannot, by

itself, be equated with a fundamental alteration of the nature and character of the

suit.
                                                                                  18


14.1. The real inquiry is whether the amendment introduces a distinct and

independent controversy having no connection with the original cause of action,

or whether it merely brings on record additional facts and consequential reliefs

having a direct nexus with the existing controversy. On the facts of the present

case, the proposed amendment falls within the latter category. The subject

matter of the proposed amendment and the original suit substantially overlap,

and the adjudication of the proposed issue would have a direct bearing upon the

title and possession claimed in respect of the suit property.



15.   The respondents have however urged that the proposed challenge to the

final decree passed in T.S. No.105 of 1998 is barred by limitation and by Order

XXIII Rule 3A of the CPC. At this stage, we are concerned with the

permissibility of the amendment and not with the ultimate merits or

maintainability of the reliefs sought to be introduced. The objections raised by

the respondents cannot therefore be finally adjudicated upon while deciding the

application for amendment, unless the proposed claim is ex facie barred in law.



16.   As regards limitation, it is well settled that a claim which is clearly barred

by limitation, particularly where its introduction would defeat an accrued right

of the opposite party, is a relevant consideration in the exercise of discretion

under Order VI Rule 17. At the same time, where the question of limitation is

itself arguable and depends upon disputed facts, including the date or manner in
                                                                                  19


which the plaintiff acquired knowledge of the relevant document or transaction,

the amendment need not necessarily be rejected at the threshold.

16.1. In Ragu Thilak D. John v. S. Rayappan and others11, this Court held that

where the plea of limitation is arguable, the amendment may be allowed and the

question of limitation be left open for determination in the suit. In Sampat

Kumar v. Ayyakannu and another12, this Court held that mere delay in seeking

amendment is not, by itself, a ground for refusing an amendment. Similarly, in

Pankaja and another v. Yellappa (Dead) by LRs and others13, this Court held

that there is no absolute rule that an amendment must be rejected merely

because the relief sought by way of amendment is alleged to be barred by

limitation; the question has to be considered in the facts and circumstances of

each case.

16.2. In the present case, the date of knowledge of the compromise decree itself

is a matter in dispute and has not been conclusively determined. The material

relied upon by the appellants, including the procurement of certified copies of

the plaint and final decree on 22.06.2020 is a circumstance requiring

consideration. It would therefore be inappropriate to finally determine the

question of limitation while considering the application for amendment. The

respondents shall remain at liberty to raise the plea of limitation before the trial

Court, which shall consider the same in accordance with law.

17.   Equally, we do not propose to pronounce upon the applicability or

otherwise of Order XXIII Rule 3A of the CPC. Whether the proposed challenge

18.   It is clarified that permitting the amendment does not amount to

acceptance of the averments incorporated therein, nor does it confer upon the

appellants any declaration or substantive right in respect of the compromise

decree. All questions relating to maintainability of the amended reliefs,

limitation, the binding nature or otherwise of the decree, the applicability of

Order XXIII Rule 3A of the CPC, title, possession and the merits of the

respective claims are expressly left open for consideration by the trial Court in

accordance with law.



19.   The objection as to prejudice also does not warrant rejection of the

amendment. The prejudice relied upon by the respondents principally arises

from the additional factual and legal issues which they would now be required

to meet. Such prejudice can adequately be addressed by permitting the
                                                                                   21


respondents to file an additional written statement and where necessary, by

imposing appropriate costs. The mere fact that an amendment requires the

opposite party to meet additional pleadings or issues does not, by itself, warrant

refusal of the amendment where the amendment is necessary for a complete and

effective adjudication of the controversy.



20.   Conversely, refusal of the amendment may result in the controversy

concerning title to the same property being fragmented into separate

proceedings, with the attendant possibility of inconsistent findings in respect of

the same parcel of land. Avoidance of such multiplicity, while preserving the

respondents’ right to contest the amended pleadings on all available grounds, is

also a relevant consideration in the exercise of jurisdiction under Order VI Rule

17 of the CPC.



21.   The decision in Basavaraj v. Indira and others (supra) does not, on the

facts of the present case, call for a different conclusion. The present case turns

upon its own facts. In particular, the disputed chain of title, the assertion that the

original plaintiff was not a party to the compromise proceedings, the subsequent

discovery of the compromise decree, and the material indicating that certified

copies of the plaint and final decree were obtained only on 22.06.2020, furnish

an explanation which cannot, at this stage, be construed as a mere omission or
                                                                               22


negligence. As indicated above, the requirement of due diligence contemplated

by the proviso to Order VI Rule 17 of the CPC stands satisfied.



22.   At the same time, the considerable delay in seeking the amendment and

the inconvenience that may be caused to the respondents cannot be disregarded.

The appropriate course therefore is to permit the amendment subject to costs,

while preserving the respondents’ right to file their additional pleadings and to

raise all objections available to them in law.
